
WeGrowHealthR takes longitudinal child growth data from raw visits to
publication tables and figures. This vignette walks through the first steps
that almost every analysis shares: describing your data to the package,
cleaning a raw export, computing z-scores and percentiles against the WHO or
CDC references, classifying nutritional status, estimating prevalence,
drawing growth charts, and tuning any plot. Each section explains the code,
the main options, what the output means and where to go next.

All examples use `growdat`, a simulated school health cohort of about 3,300
children aged 18 months to 18 years with yearly visits. It resembles a large
urban school health cohort, so the numbers look like those of the published
studies, but they are not findings.

```{r}
library(WeGrowHealthR)
head(growdat)
```

Each row is one visit. `pid` identifies the child, `site` the school site,
`dob` and `examdate` are the date of birth and the date of measurement, and
`age` is the decimal age in years.

## 1. Describe your data once with `wgh_data()`

`wgh_data()` is the data contract. You tell it which of your columns holds
each role (child identifier, sex, age or dates, height, weight, site, year)
and it returns a `wgh_data` object with standard column names that every
function in the package understands. You do this once per data set.

### Ages from dates

If you have the date of birth and the date of measurement, give them as
`dob` and `date` and leave out `age`. Age at measurement is computed as the
number of days between the two dates divided by 365.25, which is the
convention of the WHO software.

```{r}
gd <- wgh_data(growdat, id = "pid", sex = "sex", dob = "dob", date = "examdate",
               height = "height", weight = "weight", site = "site")
gd
head(gd$data)
```

Column names can be given as strings (`"pid"`) or bare names (`pid`). The
printed summary shows the number of children and visits, the age range and
the column mapping. `year` was filled from the date of measurement because
no year column was mapped, and BMI was computed from height and weight.

Dates stored as text are read with `date_format`. Here is a small data set
in which dates are written day/month/year, a common format in clinic
records:

```{r}
clinic <- data.frame(
  child = c("A", "A", "B"), gender = c("F", "F", "M"),
  birth = c("03/02/2015", "03/02/2015", "21/11/2012"),
  visit = c("10/09/2021", "12/09/2022", "15/09/2021"),
  ht = c(121.5, 127.0, 134.2), wt = c(23.1, 26.4, 31.0))
wgh_data(clinic, id = "child", sex = "gender", dob = "birth", date = "visit",
         height = "ht", weight = "wt", date_format = "%d/%m/%Y")$data
```

Sex codes such as `"F"`, `"M"`, `1` and `2`, `"girl"` and `"boy"` are
recognised and stored as `"Female"` and `"Male"`.

### Ages recorded directly

When only age is available, map it with `age`. The `age_unit` option takes
`"years"` (default), `"months"` or `"days"`. When you give both an age column
and dates, `age_from = "auto"` (default) keeps the recorded ages, fills any
missing age from the dates, and warns when a recorded age and the
date-based age differ by more than 0.1 years. That warning is a useful data
quality check. Use `age_from = "dates"` to always compute age from the dates.

```{r}
gd2 <- wgh_data(growdat, id = "pid", sex = "sex", age = "age", height = "height",
                weight = "weight", site = "site", year = "yearvisit")
wgh_map(gd2)
```

`wgh_map()` shows which original column holds each role.

**Next steps.** Pass `gd` (or `gd$data`) to any function. Most functions
also accept a plain data frame that already uses the book column names
(`pid`, `site`, `yearvisit`), so `growdat` itself works everywhere.

## 2. Clean a raw export with `wgh_clean()`

`growdat_raw` is the same cohort as a messy export from a school health
information system, with heights entered in metres, weights in grams,
height and weight swapped, duplicated visits and implausible values.

```{r}
clean <- wgh_clean(growdat_raw)
attr(clean, "cleaning_log")
```

`wgh_clean()` repairs only errors whose type is unambiguous and logs every
change. Everything else is flagged in the `implausible` column rather than
altered, so you decide what to do with it. The options `repair_units`,
`drop_duplicates` and `z_limit` switch individual steps on or off.

**Next steps.** Inspect the flagged rows with
`clean[clean$implausible, ]`, then use the cleaned data in the steps below.

## 3. Z-scores and percentiles

`wgh_add_zscores()` adds height-for-age (`haz`), weight-for-age (`waz`) and
BMI-for-age (`baz`) z-scores. With `reference = "who"` (default) it uses the
WHO 2006 Child Growth Standards below 60 months and the WHO 2007 Growth
Reference from 60 months, with the WHO restricted tails for weight and BMI.
The values agree with the `anthro` and `anthroplus` packages. With
`reference = "cdc"` it uses the CDC 2000 growth charts (2 to 20 years).
`percentiles = TRUE` adds the matching percentiles.

```{r}
z_who <- wgh_add_zscores(growdat[1:5, c("pid", "sex", "age", "height", "weight", "bmi")],
                         percentiles = TRUE)
z_who[, c("pid", "age", "haz", "haz_pct", "baz", "baz_pct")]
z_cdc <- wgh_add_zscores(growdat[1:5, c("pid", "sex", "age", "height", "weight", "bmi")],
                         reference = "cdc")
z_cdc[, c("pid", "age", "haz", "baz")]
```

The two references differ, most for BMI, because they were built from
different populations and periods. Weight-for-age is not defined by WHO
after 10 years or by CDC before 2 years, so those cells are missing.

For single values, `wgh_zscore()` takes the measurement, age, sex and
indicator. `wgh_compare_references()` shows several versions side by side,
which helps when you need to explain why two software packages disagree:

```{r}
wgh_zscore(130, age = 9, sex = "Female", indicator = "hfa")
wgh_zscore(130, age = 9, sex = "Female", indicator = "hfa", reference = "cdc")
wgh_compare_references(c(22, 28), age = c(10, 15), sex = "Male", indicator = "bfa")
```

The columns are the WHO value with restricted tails (`who`), the plain LMS
value without them (`who_plain_lms`), a symmetric approximation, the CDC
value, and the `anthroplus` value when that package is installed.

You can also give your own reference as a data frame with columns `sex`,
`age` (years), `L`, `M` and `S` (and optionally `indicator`), for example a
national growth reference.

## 4. Nutritional status with `wgh_classify()`

`wgh_classify()` adds z-scores and status categories. The WHO system
(default) uses BMI-for-age cut-offs of -3 and -2 SD for severe thinness and
thinness, +1 and +2 SD for overweight and obesity from 5 years (+2 and +3 SD
below 5 years), and HAZ below -2 (and -3) for stunting (and severe
stunting). The CDC system uses the 5th, 85th and 95th BMI percentiles.

```{r}
cl <- wgh_classify(growdat)
table(cl$bmi_status[cl$age >= 5], cl$sex[cl$age >= 5])
cl_cdc <- wgh_classify(growdat[growdat$age >= 2, ], system = "cdc")
table(cl_cdc$bmi_status, cl_cdc$sex)
```

Besides the categories, the output has indicator columns such as
`overweight_obesity`, `obesity`, `stunting` and `thinness` (TRUE or FALSE),
ready for prevalence estimation.

## 5. Prevalence and trends

`wgh_prevalence()` estimates the prevalence of an indicator, or the share of
each category of a status variable, with confidence intervals. `by` sets the
groups. For a categorical status, `method = "sison_glaz"` gives simultaneous
intervals for all categories together, as in Ho et al. (2026, Sci Rep
16:7515).

```{r}
older <- cl[cl$age >= 5, ]
wgh_prevalence(older, "bmi_status", by = "sex", method = "sison_glaz")
pv <- wgh_prevalence(older, "overweight_obesity", by = c("sex", "yearvisit"))
head(pv)
```

Each row gives the number of visits (`n`), the number with the condition
(`cases`), the prevalence in percent and its interval. A trend over
calendar time is tested with the Cochran-Armitage test:

```{r}
wgh_trend_test(older, "overweight_obesity", "yearvisit", by = "sex")
```

A small p-value says the prevalence changes steadily across years. Repeated
visits of the same child are not independent, so for formal inference on
trends use the GEE models in `wgh_gee_trend()`, which the trend flows apply
(see `vignette("trends-malnutrition")`).

```{r, fig.alt = "Overweight or obesity prevalence by year and sex"}
wgh_plot_prevalence(pv)
```

## 6. Growth charts

`wgh_plot_growth_chart()` draws a child's measurements over reference
curves. Two choices matter:

* `lines = "percentile"` (default) draws percentile curves, set with
  `centiles` (default 3, 15, 50, 85 and 97). `lines = "sd"` draws z-score
  curves, set with `sd_lines` (default -3 to +3).
* `reference = "who"` (default), `"cdc"` or your own LMS table.

`indicator` chooses height (`"hfa"`), weight (`"wfa"`) or BMI (`"bfa"`),
and `age_range` the ages shown.

```{r, fig.alt = "WHO height-for-age percentiles with one girl's measurements"}
girl <- growdat$pid[growdat$sex == "Female"][1]
wgh_plot_growth_chart(growdat, ids = girl)
```

```{r, fig.alt = "WHO height-for-age SD curves with one girl's measurements"}
wgh_plot_growth_chart(growdat, ids = girl, lines = "sd")
```

```{r, fig.alt = "CDC BMI-for-age percentiles with a shaded band"}
wgh_plot_growth_chart(growdat, ids = girl, indicator = "bfa", reference = "cdc",
                      centiles = c(5, 50, 85, 95), band = TRUE)
```

The CDC BMI chart marks the 85th and 95th percentiles, the CDC cut-offs for
overweight and obesity. Several children can be shown together, each in its
own colour, with `child_colour = NULL`:

```{r, fig.alt = "Three girls on one chart"}
three <- unique(growdat$pid[growdat$sex == "Female"])[1:3]
wgh_plot_growth_chart(growdat, ids = three, child_colour = NULL, age_range = c(2, 14))
```

**Next steps.** To judge whether a child's growth follows the expected
course given the child's own history, rather than the population, use the
conditional references in `vignette("growth-distributions")`.

## 7. Tuning any plot

Every plot function and `plot()` method in the package accepts the same
display options through `...`. They are documented in `?wgh_plot_options`:
titles and axis labels, `base_size`, `legend` position, a `palette`,
`point_size`, `line_width`, `alpha`, `show_ci`, facets and axis limits.

```{r, fig.alt = "The prevalence plot restyled"}
wgh_plot_prevalence(pv, title = "Overweight or obesity, 5 to 18 years",
                    palette = c(Male = "black", Female = "grey55"),
                    show_ci = FALSE, y_limits = c(0, 50), base_size = 12, legend = "right")
```

To use the same settings for several plots, build them once:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
opts <- wgh_plot_options(base_size = 9, legend = "none")
do.call(wgh_plot_prevalence, c(list(pv), opts))
```

Plots are ggplot objects, so you can also add any ggplot2 layer, scale or
theme, and save them with `wgh_save_figure()` (TIFF and PDF at 600 dpi by
default, the format most journals ask for).

## 8. Tracking the analytic sample

Analyses usually restrict the data step by step. `wgh_sample_flow()` records
how many children and visits remain after each step and, when there is a
`site` column, the share retained at each site. A step that removes one site
much more than the others is flagged, because it can bias comparisons.

```{r}
fl <- wgh_sample_flow(growdat,
  "Ages 5 to 18" = ~ age >= 5 & age <= 18.5,
  "At least 3 visits" = wgh_min_visits(3))
fl
```

```{r, fig.alt = "Children retained at each step by site"}
plot(fl)
```

The restricted data are in `fl$data`.

## 9. Run modes, reports and export

Heavy functions read their defaults (bootstrap replicates, folds, quantile
grids, subsample sizes) from a run mode. `wgh_config("dev")` gives settings
that run in seconds for checking code, `"analysis"` is the default and
`"publication"` uses full grids and bootstraps. Any argument you pass
explicitly overrides the mode, and single settings can be overridden with
`wgh_config("analysis", B = 1000)`.

```{r}
old <- wgh_config("dev")
wgh_opt("B")
```

The study workflows (`wgh_flow_*()`) return a `wgh_report` that holds every
table, figure and model of one study, the analytic sample flow and the
status of each model (fitted, failed or skipped, with the reason).

```{r}
rep <- wgh_flow_malnutrition_trends(growdat, mode = "dev")
rep
```

```{r, eval = FALSE}
rep$tables$prevalence_by_year        # a table
plot(rep, "fig_trends", base_size = 13)       # a figure, restyled
wgh_export(rep, "malnutrition_results")       # Excel workbook, TIFF and PDF figures
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
wgh_config(old)
```

## Where to go next

* `vignette("trends-malnutrition")`: secular trends, prevalence, the double
  burden of malnutrition and GEE trend models.
* `vignette("trajectories")`: how a prepubertal exposure relates to later
  height trajectories with mixed models.
* `vignette("growth-curves")`: SITAR growth curves, the pubertal spurt,
  its timing, intensity and duration.
* `vignette("growth-distributions")`: quantile regression, growth
  inequality and conditional growth references.
* `vignette("phenotypes-states")`: growth phenotypes, canalization and
  multistate models.
* `vignette("prediction")`: predicting late-adolescent height and
  explaining predictions.
* `vignette("simulated-data")` and `vignette("reproducing-the-program")`,
  which runs all 14 study flows.
* `vignette("parallel-computing")`: running bootstraps, quantile grids and
  cross-validation on several cores with identical results.

`wgh_references()` lists the studies whose analyses the package reproduces.
